newsitem.title: GREECE: FOCUS - PIG RATTLES ATHENS BOURSE BUT NEW ERA COMING.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - PIG RATTLES ATHENS BOURSE BUT NEW ERA COMING.

text.p: PIG -- panic, ignorance, greed -- it was all there during the week that shook the Athens bourse and threatened to bring down the house.
Was it an earthquake or simply a shock? The Delta Securities scandal helped expose the bourse's dirty underwear and brokers now see a new era unfolding that should mean a better market.

This, they say, is not going to be fast and it won't be painless. They predict in a year or two many of the bourse's 65 members will be out of the business, leaving around 20 stronger, better capitalised players.
"In a couple of years we will witness a dramatic fall in the number of brokerages to around 20 strong players," said the chief executive of a large securities firm.
Beyond the intricacies of the Delta settlement scandal -- who was behind it, how the scam mechanisms backfired -- there is a greater meaning, brokers say.

"The market's healthy forces realised that the system was in danger of blowing up. The story has just begun. Our stock market won't fall back, it will move forward and improve," a seasoned broker told Reuters.

"This means it is now time to say good-bye to the bourse we knew during 1991-96. We will slowly say hello to a new market," he said, refering to a free-wheeling period which saw the number of brokerages and listings expand.
HOW THE CRISIS DEVELOPED

Citing systematic abuse of poor supervision and loopholes in clearing mechanisms, brokers who played by the book realised they were the losers of a notorious short-selling practice which kept the market locked in a depressed range.

"The pressure on the press to slam the bourse's ills was not accidental. It came from healthy forces who realised many were making money on their backs and to the detriment of the stock market," said an experienced broker on condition of anonymity.

This, in turn, forced regulatory authorities to clamp down and Delta's 2.6 billion drachma settlement default came to the fore last week. It opened a Pandora's box of problems amid cries of cover-up by the brokers association.

"A war amid the brokerage community has started, a war that is bound to continue. Many reacted because they realised they were being taken advantage of, the system was being abused," another broker said.

He said it all boils down to brokers deciding to fight it out for survival. The government, surprised and spooked by the crisis, wanted to get the bourse working again fast, fearing wider economic repercussions.
SHORT SELLING PRACTICES THE HEART OF THE PROBLEM

Watching the bourse bleed on Thursday, its first day out of intensive care and down 3.31 percent, many brokers still feared other aspects of short selling practices, beyond settlement with the clearing house.

Although many members appeared to be OK on their settlements with the clearing house, concerns were being expressed that some were still open vis-a-vis their clients, having used clients' shares to deliver on previous short sales.
Thus, part of the compromise with the government was that international auditing firms would step in to look into this.

Athens has long cried out for regulated short-selling but authorities have proved slow on the matter and happy to turn a blind eye. When playing by the book, the only way to play Greek equities was to play it long.
But with commissions deregulated and a flat, depressed market it was an anaemic proposition, unable to sustain 65 brokerages.
Short selling developed into a way to boost turnover, make fast money on the downside and even to break even on previous losses. But it wasn't fair play -- it wasn't available to all.
"When commissions were liberalised it became obvious that the Athens stock exchange could no longer provide enough income for 65 brokers," said ING Barings in a recent report.
"We have therefore been expecting some smaller brokers to go out of business at some point. Obviously, they are unwilling to exit gracefully," it added.
ING Barings figured the average daily volume was about $30 million. A rough average suggests each of the 65 brokers earned only $30,000 of gross commission income per month.
"Since 30 percent of the market is controlled by the top five brokers, the monthly average revenue of most brokers is actually substantially lower," it said.

The case for a crowding out in the brokerage community is also fueled by the recent national economy and capital market commission warning that they may increase brokers' assessments to boost the exchange's guarantee fund.
Such a move would aim to avert a new Delta scandal. But it would not be music to the ears of many brokers.

"If the current 6.0 billion drachma guarantee fund is raised substantially, quite a few brokers will not be able to afford the higher assessments. They will find themselves out of the industry, hors-de-combat," comments one market watcher.
The shake out is coming. It is just the beginning, he said.
--George Georgiopoulos, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
